notes:
I have gathered substantial material from multiple traditions. Here are the verse-by-verse notes.

---

## 1 Chronicles 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Verse 1

- **v. 1 — Traditional Reading:** David consulted his military leaders — the commanders of thousands and hundreds and every chief (nagîd). This consultation is unique to Chronicles; the parallel in 2 Samuel 6:1 simply notes David gathered 30,000 chosen men. Notably, the text says David consulted with the leaders but **not** with the LORD Himself. This omission becomes the root of the tragedy that follows.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 1 — Ellicott:** This consultation occurred some time after the coronation at Hebron. The "captains of hundreds" represented the smaller military divisions of each tribe. The chiefs together constituted the Great Council of the nation.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/13.htm

- **v. 1 — Gill:** The consultation was held with the chiliarchs and centurions of the large armed body from every tribe who had met to crown David king. Gill notes that Dr. Lightfoot observed the actual moving of the ark did not happen until considerably later, after Hiram's embassy, the capture of Jerusalem, and the two battles with the Philistines.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/13.htm

---

### Verse 2

- **v. 2 — Traditional Reading:** David addressed the whole assembly, phrasing his proposal conditionally — "If it seems good to you, and if this is of the LORD." This shows both deference to the people and a stated desire to do God's will. Yet David failed to actually seek the LORD's counsel. The invitation went out to "the rest of our brothers" — those Israelites who remained after the Philistine oppressions — and specifically to the priests and Levites in their pastureland cities.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 2 — Ellicott:** The Hebrew phrasing "and if it be from Jehovah" is not dependent on the first clause; David says "If before you the thing be good, and if the motion come from Jehovah." The expression "let us send abroad" is literally "break we forth, send we" — meaning to send with all despatch. The "congregation of Israel" here refers to the Council of Chiefs (30,000 in Samuel's account).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/13.htm

- **v. 2 — Gill:** David calls the common people "our brethren," showing humility. Gill notes this as a type: as David owned the people as his brethren, so Christ is not ashamed to call His people brethren (Hebrews 2:11).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/13.htm

- **v. 2 — Reformed (Ligonier):** The Chronicler uses the same word for "assembly of Israel" that is used for the community gathered for worship. The decision to bring the ark to Jerusalem was motivated by a desire to centralize the true worship of God's people. The Chronicler emphasizes proper worship because he wrote after the exile and wanted the postexilic community not to repeat preexilic mistakes.
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blessing-and-curse-of-the-ark

---

### Verse 3

- **v. 3 — Traditional Reading:** David's goal is to "bring back the ark of our God." The ark had been neglected during Saul's reign; they "did not inquire of Him" (or "did not seek it"). This is a sad commentary on Saul's spiritual indifference — for some 20 years the ark sat in obscurity at Abinadab's house in Kiriath-jearim while the nation went without seeking God's presence.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 3 — Ellicott:** The Hebrew verb means "bring round" — to transfer the ark from Kiriath-jearim to Jerusalem, just as the throne was transferred (same verb) from Saul to David. Ellicott notes the translation "we sought it not" fits better than "we inquired not at it," since there is no clear evidence the ark itself was ever used as an oracle. It may also be translated "we sought Him not," referring the suffix to God (cf. 1 Chronicles 15:13).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/13.htm

- **v. 3 — Gill:** Saul was "indifferent to religion, and careless about it"; the people were content with worship at the tabernacle at Gibeah, even though the token of the divine Presence was absent.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/13.htm

- **v. 3 — G. Campbell Morgan (quoted at Precept Austin):** David knew that not he, but Jehovah, was Israel's true King. His own rule had to depend upon the will and counsel of God. The people also needed to recognize this, hence his determination to bring in the ark.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 3 — Constable (Evangelical):** David's desire to bring the ark into Jerusalem showed his concern that God would dwell among His people and that they would again have ritual access to God — something they had not had during Saul's reign.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-13.html

---

### Verse 4

- **v. 4 — Traditional Reading:** The whole assembly unanimously agreed, "for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people." This is the critical flaw: what is right in the eyes of people is not necessarily right in the eyes of God. The Chronicler echoes the dark days of Judges when "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25). Majority opinion does not determine God's will.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 4 — Gill:** The people "saw the propriety, necessity, and usefulness of it." Their motives were good; the flaw was in the method, not the goal.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/13.htm

---

### Verse 5

- **v. 5 — Traditional Reading:** David assembled "all Israel" from the far south (Shihor of Egypt, the Wadi el-Arish) to the far north (Lebo-hamath). This was a national event of the highest order, demonstrating David's desire to unify the entire nation around the worship of God. The assembly was enormous — Samuel records 30,000 chosen men.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 5 — Ellicott:** Shihor of Egypt is the winter torrent that formed the boundary between Egypt and Canaan (modern Wady el-Arish). Hamath was the usual designation of the northern boundary of Palestine — an ancient independent kingdom friendly to David.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/13.htm

- **v. 5 — Gill:** Shihor refers to the Nile (so the Targum and Jewish writers), called Shihor from the blackness of its water (cf. Jeremiah 2:18). The gathering ran from south to north across the full extent of Israel's territory.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/13.htm

---

### Verse 6

- **v. 6 — Traditional Reading:** They went to Baalah (another name for Kiriath-jearim, "city of woods," also called Kirjath-baal), which belonged to Judah. The ark is described as that of "the LORD, who is enthroned between the cherubim — the ark that is called by the Name." This rich theological description emphasizes that the ark was the earthly throne of the invisible God, the place where His presence dwelled.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

- **v. 6 — Ellicott:** "Baalah" means "Baal's town" and was likely the original Canaanite name. "The LORD, who sitteth upon the cherubim" is a standard OT title. The phrase "which is called Name" reflects the later Israelite practice of avoiding pronouncing the divine name Jehovah, substituting "the Name" (hashshēm). Some manuscripts read "there" (shām) instead of "name" (shēm), yielding "who is invoked there."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/13.htm

- **v. 6 — Constable:** "In a real sense Yahweh was wherever His Ark was. It crystallized His immanence, bearing witness to both His nearness and His sovereignty" (quoting Merrill). The ark was not merely a symbol; it was the actual place God had chosen to reside among His people (Exodus 25:22).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-13.html

---

### Verse 7

- **v. 7 — Traditional Reading:** They carried the ark on a **new cart**, driven by Uzzah and Ahio, sons of Abinadab. This was directly contrary to God's command. The ark was designed with rings and poles specifically so it could be carried on the shoulders of Levites from the family of Kohath (Exodus 25:12–15; Numbers 4:15). The Philistines had used a cart to return the ark (1 Samuel 6:7–11), and Israel copied their method — a pagan innovation — rather than obeying God's Word.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 7 — F.B. Meyer (quoted at Enduring Word):** "There it was expressly ordained that the Ark should be carried on the shoulders of the priests, because the cause of God must proceed through the world by the means of consecrated men, rather than by mechanical instrumentality."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

- **v. 7 — G. Campbell Morgan:** "The long neglect of the Ark may have rendered these men unfamiliar with the very explicit commands concerning the method of its removal. Or they may have grown careless as to the importance of attending to such details."
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 7 — Matthew Henry (via Precept Austin):** "When after long disuse ordinances come to be revived, it is too common for even wise and good men to make some mistakes. Who would have thought that David should have made such a blunder as this, to carry the ark upon a cart? … We must walk by rule, not by example, when it varies from the rule; no, not those examples that providence has owned."
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 7 — Uzzah and Ahio's names:** "Uzza" means "strength" and "Ahio" means "friendly" — a vivid picture of much service done for God: impressive, energetic, and well-intentioned, but not according to His revealed will.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

---

### Verse 8

- **v. 8 — Traditional Reading:** David and all Israel celebrated "with all their might" — singing, harps, lyres, tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets. It was a magnificent, joyful, high-energy worship production. Yet God was not pleased, because the entire enterprise was conducted in disobedience. This exposes a dangerous tendency: we judge worship by how it makes us feel, not by whether it pleases God according to His Word.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

- **v. 8 — Spurgeon (quoted at Enduring Word and Precept Austin):** "If you read the story through, you will see that it appears to be an affair of singing, and harps, and psalteries, and timbrels, and cymbals, and trumpets, and of a new cart and cattle; that is about all there is in it. There is not even a mention of humiliation of heart, or of solemn awe in the presence of that God of whom the ark was but the outward symbol. I am afraid that this first attempt was too much after the will of the Flesh, and the energy of nature."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 8 — Spurgeon's further analysis (Precept Austin):** Despite the multitudes, the pomp, the energy, there was "no thought as to God's mind," "more music than grace," "the priests were not in their places, nor the Levites to carry the ark: oxen took the place of willing men," "there was no sacrifice," and "there was little reverence." Spurgeon asks pointedly: "Are all the observances and practices of our churches scriptural? Are not some of them purely will-worship?"
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 8 — Constable:** "Even though there was much joy and worship as the people transported the ark, they did not obey God's orders for its proper treatment … Worship can never replace obedience to God's revealed will (cf. 1 Samuel 15:22-23)."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-13.html

- **v. 8 — Ellicott:** The Hebrew verb translated "played" means "were dancing (to music)." The Chronicler's text differs from Samuel, which has "with all woods of cypresses" (likely a scribal error). The LXX of Samuel reads "in strength," matching the sense here.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/13.htm

---

### Verse 9

- **v. 9 — Traditional Reading:** At the threshing floor of Chidon (called Nachon in 2 Samuel 6:6), the oxen stumbled. Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark to steady it. A threshing floor is where wheat and chaff are separated — symbolically, God was about to separate the chaff from their disobedient worship. Uzzah's instinctive action seemed reasonable and helpful, yet Numbers 4:15 expressly forbade touching any holy thing on penalty of death.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 9 — Ellicott:** "Chidon" in Chronicles versus "Nachon" in Samuel — the latter is probably original. The Targum, Syriac, and Arabic of Samuel treat nākûn as a participle meaning "prepared threshing floor." The verb "stumbled" may also mean "plunged" (used transitively in 2 Kings 9:33, "Throw her down").
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/13.htm

---

### Verse 10

- **v. 10 — Traditional Reading:** The anger of the LORD burned against Uzzah, and God struck him dead — "because he had put his hand on the ark." He died "before God." God fulfilled the warning of Numbers 4:15. David wanted Israel to know the presence of the LORD, and God did show up — but in judgment, not blessing. Uzzah's sin was more than a reflex; it revealed critical errors: (1) he thought it didn't matter who handled the ark, (2) he thought God couldn't protect the ark Himself, and (3) he considered his hand holier than the ground.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

- **v. 10 — Alexander Maclaren (quoted at Enduring Word):** "He saw no difference between the ark and any other valuable article. His intention to help was right enough; but there was a profound insensibility to the awful sacredness of the ark, on which even its Levitical bearers were forbidden to lay hands."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

- **v. 10 — Reformed (Ligonier):** "The failure of the Israelites to follow the directions of worship led to the cursing of Uzzah … The Lord takes His worship seriously. We are not allowed to treat God with irreverence by ignoring what He has commanded regarding worship, and if we do so, there may be severe consequences. Let us seek to be faithful to the Lord as we praise Him, worshiping Him according to the Scriptures."
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blessing-and-curse-of-the-ark

- **v. 10 — Constable:** The writer's intended lesson is that "Yahweh is holy and His people should not take His presence among them lightly (cf. Leviticus 10:1–11; Numbers 16). … It would have been tempting to regard the rituals and physical objects used in worship as common. The writer warned his readers not to make this fatal mistake."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-13.html

---

### Verse 11

- **v. 11 — Traditional Reading:** David became angry — "because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah." This anger likely mixed confusion, grief, and perhaps self-directed frustration. David could not understand why his good intentions were not enough. He named the place Perez-uzzah ("the bursting forth against Uzzah"), and this name remained as a permanent reminder.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

- **v. 11 — Precept Austin:** David may have been angry primarily with himself, knowing he should have consulted God and followed the Law. As king, he was to write out a copy of the Law and read it all his days (Deuteronomy 17:18–20); had he done so, the tragedy would have been averted.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 11 — Spurgeon (Precept Austin):** "We are too apt to be displeased with God because he is displeased with us." David's own sense of unworthiness for such holy work made him cry out in the next verse.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

---

### Verse 12

- **v. 12 — Traditional Reading:** David's anger turned to fear. "How can I ever bring the ark of God to me?" This was the right response — holy fear. Yet David need not have feared God Himself; the problem lay in his own failure to obey. David's question is answered later (chapter 15): "To the law and to the testimony!" (cf. Isaiah 8:20). God's Word told him exactly how the ark should be brought.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

- **v. 12 — Spurgeon:** "David was afraid of God that day" — some make the holiness of God and the strictness of His rule "an excuse for wicked neglect. Others are overwhelmed with holy fear; and therefore pause a while, till they are better prepared for the holy service." David's fear was reverent and led to preparation, not abandonment.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **v. 12 — Selman (quoted at Enduring Word):** "If Chronicles' readers wanted Israel's former glories restored, they too must reckon with a God whose dynamic holiness could not be contained within human limitations."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

---

### Verse 13

- **v. 13 — Traditional Reading:** Instead of bringing the ark to the City of David, David diverted it to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. This was not random — Obed-edom was a Levite of the clan of Kohath, of the family of Korah (1 Chronicles 26:4), the very family God commanded to transport and care for the ark (Numbers 4:15). David, perhaps unknowingly, ended up doing what the Law required.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

- **v. 13 — Ellicott:** "Obed-edom the Gittite" — since 1 Chronicles 26:1–4 identifies Obed-edom as a Korhitic Levite, "Gittite" is generally taken to mean a native of Gath-rimmon, a Levitical township (Joshua 21:24) belonging to the clan of Kohath, which was charged with carriage of the ark.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/13.htm

- **v. 13 — Adam Clarke (via Enduring Word):** Clarke suggests Obed-edom was a Levite who had merely been sojourning at Gath, hence the term "Gittite." He was not a Philistine but a proper Levite.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

- **v. 13 — Reformed (Ligonier):** After God struck Uzzah, David "had it taken to the house of Obed-edom … But God blessed the house of Obed-edom while the ark was present, indicating that His curse was not inevitable in the presence of the ark. This convinced David that he should move forward in bringing the ark into Jerusalem."
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ark-comes-to-jerusalem

---

### Verse 14

- **v. 14 — Traditional Reading:** The ark stayed with Obed-edom's family for three months, and "the LORD blessed his household and everything he owned." When God's Word was obeyed and His holiness was respected, blessing followed. The curse at Perez-uzzah did not come from God's heart but from human disobedience. The contrast is stark: Uzzah touched the ark in disobedience and died; Obed-edom housed the ark in obedience and was blessed.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

- **v. 14 — Constable:** "Where God's presence abode there was power, as always." The blessing on Obed-edom demonstrated that the ark itself was not the problem; the problem was irreverent handling.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-13.html

- **v. 14 — Ellicott:** "The ark of God remained with the family (lit. 'by the house') of Obed-edom … in its own house (shrine)." Samuel simply says "the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his house." For the nature of the blessing, see 1 Chronicles 26:4–8, where Obed-edom's descendants are listed as capable men and gatekeepers.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/13.htm

- **v. 14 — Reformed (Ligonier):** "The actual presence of the ark was a source of blessing for an obedient people, as seen in the blessings that came to the house of Obed-edom."
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blessing-and-curse-of-the-ark

## Summary of Points Where Traditions Differ

The sources I found are broadly agreed on the meaning of this chapter. No sharp denominational divide emerged; the lesson that God cares about both the *goal* and the *method* of worship is universal across the traditions represented.

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasises that emotional, high-energy worship ("with all their might") can still displease God if done in disobedience. The presence of music, celebration, and intensity does not guarantee God's approval. This speaks directly to charismatic worship culture.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-13/

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Stresses the "regulative principle" of worship — that God must be worshipped only according to His commands in Scripture. The ark episode illustrates that "the Lord takes His worship seriously" and "we are not allowed to treat God with irreverence by ignoring what He has commanded regarding worship."
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blessing-and-curse-of-the-ark

- **Baptist (Spurgeon, via Precept Austin):** Spurgeon applies the lesson directly to church practice, asking whether all observances in our churches are scriptural or "purely will-worship." He highlights the absence of sacrifice, prayer, and reverence, seeing the episode as a warning against "the will of the Flesh, and the energy of nature."
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-13-commentary

- **Evangelical (Constable):** Emphasises the theological point that worship can never replace obedience, citing 1 Samuel 15:22–23. The Chronicler's postexilic audience needed to learn that "Yahweh is holy and His people should not take His presence among them lightly."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-13.html
